title: What will more intelligence actually do for us?
gist: Noah Smith concedes that superintelligence has arrived — an AI model disproved the 87-year-old Jacobian Conjecture and Terence Tao needed AI's help to understand the solution — yet employment and productivity look nearly unchanged, and he takes seriously the hypothesis that intelligence itself has diminishing returns. His investable conclusion is that AI's productivity payoff will come from three non-intelligence channels: replicability of cognitive capital, the dissolution of distributed tacit-knowledge moats like Zeiss optics and Chinese rare-earth refining, and 'cloud laws' — regularities too diffuse for humans to communicate but exploitable by machines.

insights.claim: An AI model disproved the Jacobian Conjecture, an 87-year-old open problem human mathematicians had struggled with, AI solved an important open question in quantum cryptography, and solving Erdos problems has become almost child's play for the best models.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Frontier research-grade math is now a solved category, which resets expectations for AI in any domain with smooth, verifiable solution spaces — including quantitative research and code.
insights.locator: Not a lot of people expected that AI would come for the mathematicians

insights.claim: AI came for mathematicians before truck drivers: the greatest living human mathematician turned to AI to understand a proof, while long-distance trucking employment is slightly higher than it was a decade ago.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Automation risk does not track wage level or perceived cognitive difficulty — physical-world jobs have proven far stickier than elite cognitive ones, which inverts the standard labour-displacement trade.
insights.quote: Meanwhile, long-distance trucking employment is slightly higher than it was a decade ago.
insights.locator: Not a lot of people expected that AI would come for the mathematicians

insights.claim: AGI or ASI is here by any reasonable definition, yet the world remains much the same: there is a huge data center boom and most people use AI daily, but people still commute, sit in front of computers and collect paychecks.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The gap between demonstrated capability and realized economic transformation is the central AI trade — it argues against pricing near-term GDP discontinuity while the compute buildout continues regardless.
insights.quote: “AGI”, or “ASI”, or whatever you want to call it, is certainly here. And yet…the world remains much the same.
insights.locator: It’s still possible to find some mental tasks

insights.claim: Despite entering the intelligence explosion, employment has not been disrupted in a significant way — people are staying in their jobs longer — and productivity growth has been decently robust but nothing amazing.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The macro data do not yet validate either the mass-unemployment or the productivity-boom narrative, so both AI-labour-shock and AI-productivity-miracle positions are currently unsupported by aggregates.
insights.locator: There’s a huge data center boom

insights.claim: Practitioners are openly surprised by the anticlimax — Clifford Sosin's test is to talk to Fable 5 for an hour and then to your ten smartest friends, concluding that superintelligence arrived and turned out to be incremental, with no takeoff and no explosion.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Sentiment among sophisticated AI observers is shifting from imminent-singularity to incremental-diffusion, which usually precedes a repricing of narrative-driven AI premia.
insights.quote: Superintelligence arrived. You probably didn’t notice, because it turned out to be kind of incremental
insights.locator: And Clifford Sosin writes

insights.claim: Francois Chollet argues intelligence is not an unbounded scalar like height but a conversion ratio with an optimality bound — increasing it is less like making a tower taller and more like making a ball rounder, where past a point every improvement is marginal.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: If intelligence saturates, scaling compute buys progressively less capability per dollar — the core risk to valuations premised on unbounded capability growth.
insights.quote: Intelligence is a conversion ratio, with an optimality bound. Increasing intelligence is not so much like "making the tower taller", it's more like "making the ball rounder".
insights.locator: One of the biggest misconceptions people have about intelligence

insights.claim: Machines' advantages beyond intelligence — greater processing speed, unlimited working memory, perfect recall — are mostly things humans can already access through externalized cognitive tools, which weakens the case that machine cognition will run away from human cognition.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The bear case for AI exceptionalism rests on this substitution claim; the author later argues against it, so which side is right determines whether AI is a tool or a new factor of production.
insights.locator: Now of course smart humans aren't quite at the optimal bound

insights.claim: Humans may be extremely specialized near the theoretical maximum in a few narrow tasks — extracting patterns from sparse data, synthesizing them into intuition and judgement, and communicating them in language — which explains why AI leapt ahead in math, coding and forecasting while the chatbot interface does not feel much smarter.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Predicts capability gains keep concentrating in verifiable technical domains rather than judgement and taste, which is where AI product revenue will and will not accrue.
insights.locator: It seems possible that humans are simply incredibly specialized

insights.claim: Talking to Terence Tao about math feels superhuman but talking to him about lunch or movies sounds like a fairly smart normal guy — AI will surpass Tao at math but may never get much better than thoughtful humans at recommendation and everyday judgement, because it may not be mathematically possible.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Caps the upside for AI in taste-and-preference businesses (media recommendation, curation) while leaving technical-domain upside intact.
insights.locator: It would also explain why when you talk to Terence Tao

insights.claim: If intelligence is the ability to extract information from data, then even an infinitely advanced model with infinite compute is bounded by the finite information available in the data — and data supply is itself limited by our inherently finite ability to measure the world.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Makes instrumentation and measurement — sensors, data acquisition — the binding constraint rather than compute, redirecting where the scarce input actually sits.
insights.quote: You can’t transform the world unless you can (in some generalized sense) understand it, and you can’t understand the world unless you can measure it
insights.locator: Why would intelligence top out like this?

insights.claim: Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor argue there are relatively few real-world cognitive tasks where human limitations are telling enough for AI to blow past human performance as it does in chess, because many domains have high irreducible error and humans already sit near that limit.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Irreducible error sets a ceiling on AI's value in stochastic domains — an argument for concentrating AI investment in verifiable, low-noise workflows.
insights.locator: This is basically the hypothesis advanced by Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor

insights.claim: Narayanan and Kapoor predict AI will not meaningfully outperform trained humans — particularly teams of humans augmented with simple automated tools — at forecasting geopolitical events such as elections.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A directly testable prediction against AI-driven forecasting and prediction-market products; human-plus-tool teams remain the benchmark to beat.
insights.quote: We predict that AI will not be able to meaningfully outperform trained humans (particularly teams of humans and especially if augmented with simple automated tools) at forecasting geopolitical events (say elections).
insights.locator: We predict that AI will not be able to meaningfully outperform

insights.claim: Clifford Sosin's framing is that we hold a thin scatter of facts and reasoning fills the space between them: where that space behaves well — coding, math, most administrative work, with smooth solution spaces and tractable verification — AI is close to godlike, but the binding limit is contact with reality because a smarter reasoner does not produce new facts.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Gives a screen for which workflows AI will actually eat: smooth solution space plus cheap verification — precisely the software, math and back-office categories already being disrupted.
insights.quote: The limit is contact with reality. A smarter reasoner fills the gaps between known facts in simple areas faster and better, but it doesn't produce new facts.
insights.locator: Sosin says something similar

insights.claim: Even with infinite data collection, chaos can make the cost of extracting additional information explode — in a deterministic universe, the tiniest measurement error in the present still blows up into huge error when extrapolating even a small distance into the future.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Chaos, not data scarcity, may be the real ceiling on AI prediction — bearish for AI-driven macro and weather-style forecasting claims, neutral for AI in control and optimization.
insights.locator: Sosin makes an important point here

insights.claim: The most important advantage of machine superintelligence is replicability: the number of human intelligences is fixed by a fertility rate that is falling inexorably, whereas building more data centers with more compute produces more parallel agents and therefore more cognitive work.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Reframes compute as reproducible physical capital rather than a research input — the strongest structural argument for sustained data center capex even if capability gains flatten.
insights.locator: The most obvious advantage that machine superintelligence confers is replicability.

insights.claim: Cognitive capacity becomes good old physical capital that, unlike human capital, can simply be built more of whenever you like by reinvesting a portion of economic output — analogous to suddenly discovering how to manufacture more land in any city on the planet.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: If cognition is reproducible capital, the returns accrue to whoever finances and owns the compute stack, not to scarce talent — a fundamental shift in where AI rents settle.
insights.quote: It’s good old physical capital; unlike human capital, you can just build more of it whenever you like
insights.locator: It’s not free, but nor is it limited.

insights.claim: The push into robotics, world models and physical AI has a major tailwind from the battery revolution, which allows energy to be stored and moved around much more easily — the physical tools for turning dumb matter into smart matter arrived alongside the digital ones.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Links the robotics investment cycle to battery cost curves, making energy storage a gating input for embodied AI rather than an unrelated sector.
insights.locator: Of course, lots of tasks are physical ones

insights.claim: Intelligence in robots is divisible in a way human intelligence is not: a robot the size of an ant can be remotely controlled by a data center the size of a football field.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Decoupling actuator size from cognitive capacity opens form factors impossible for human labour — watch for micro-robotics and teleoperated fleets rather than humanoid analogues.
insights.locator: It’s also worth noting that like the energy in batteries

insights.claim: The long-run steady state is a higher capital-to-labor ratio in which each human leverages an army of intelligent machines — basically another industrial revolution, and one that has very little to do with whether AI beats human intelligence head-to-head.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The bull case survives even if the diminishing-returns hypothesis is true, which means AI-infrastructure exposure does not require betting on capability takeoff.
insights.locator: In the long-run steady state

insights.claim: Zeiss makes the mirrors for ASML's EUV chipmaking machines to a tolerance where, if a mirror were the size of Germany, the biggest bump would be one millimeter high — and no one, including the people at Zeiss, knows exactly how they do it.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Quantifies why the EUV supply chain is un-replicable and therefore why export controls on it bind — the durability of that moat is now an open question.
insights.quote: If one of the mirrors that Zeiss makes for ASML’s EUV chipmaking machines were the size of Germany, the biggest bump on that mirror would be just one millimeter high.
insights.locator: The German company Zeiss makes the best glass on the planet.

insights.claim: Zeiss's technology cannot be stolen because it is tacit and distributed — a vast number of little tricks spread across many employees who do not always realize what they are doing, so the knowledge exists at the level of the organization rather than in any blueprint or any individual's head.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Identifies the only genuinely un-hackable moat — organization-level tacit process knowledge — as distinct from patents or trade secrets that Huawei took from Cisco and Nortel.
insights.locator: Zeiss’ technology basically can’t be stolen

insights.claim: China can cut off rare-earth supply at will largely because other countries are bad at refining them — separating rare earths requires a ton of little chemistry tricks that Chinese refiners spent four decades accumulating, so American or Japanese refiners cannot replicate the cost structure overnight.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Explains why Western rare-earth projects keep failing on cost rather than geology — process knowledge, not mineral access, is the bottleneck to de-risking the supply chain.
insights.locator: A big part of the reason China can cut off the supply of rare earths

insights.claim: Instrumenting workers with smart glasses, gloves and plant-wide sensors would let AI synthesize the data and rapidly suggest small process improvements, running fast cycles of experimentation that could dissolve tacit-knowledge barriers — and this capability depends only on handling huge amounts of data quickly, not on AI's raw intelligence.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A concrete mechanism by which Western refining and advanced manufacturing could close cost gaps with China — watch industrial-sensor and process-optimization deployments as the leading indicator.
insights.locator: Except in the age of AI, this might change.

insights.claim: If AI erodes distributed tacit knowledge as a barrier to diffusion, lagging firms catch up to leading firms much faster, raising economy-wide productivity and competition and creating more consumer surplus — but possibly reducing the incentive to innovate by making technology less excludable.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A direct threat to the moats behind quality-compounder valuations: faster diffusion compresses the excess returns of leading firms even as it lifts aggregate output.
insights.locator: This could improve economy-wide productivity

insights.claim: If any company could optimize any production process five times faster than today, the whole economy would speed up as components got cheaper, turnaround times and product cycles shortened, and scale-up got much faster.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Frames the productivity upside as cycle-time compression rather than headcount reduction — the metric to track is time-to-scale, not labour cost per unit.
insights.locator: Imagine if any company could optimize any production process five times faster

themes.theme: Cloud laws and a new scientific method

insights.claim: Decades of natural language processing research failed to find the principles behind human linguistic communication, then LLMs made it a solved problem — they reliably sound human even though no one understands how they manage it.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Proof of concept that a domain can be mastered technologically without being understood scientifically — the template for where AI creates value next.
insights.locator: For decades, researchers in the field of natural language processing

insights.claim: 'Cloud laws' are causal regularities that technology can exploit but that are too diffuse and complex for an individual human to intuit or communicate — human language obeys them, and candidates include economics, sociology, political science, plasma, topological materials and aerial turbulence.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Names the specific domains where AI could produce controllable technology without theory — fusion plasma control and advanced materials are the investable near-term instances.
insights.quote: I call these “cloud laws” — causal regularities that can be exploited by technology, but which are too diffuse and complex for an individual human being to either intuit or communicate.
insights.locator: Another way of saying this is that there may be laws of the universe

insights.claim: If cloud laws are widespread, we are on the precipice of a scientific renaissance that would amount to a whole new scientific revolution — reliably controlling complex phenomena without ever reducing them to textbook principles.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The high-upside scenario for AI's economic impact runs through discovery in complex physical systems rather than through labour substitution.
insights.locator: What if there are lots of other aspects of the Universe

insights.claim: Chollet is wrong that groups of humans using pre-AI computing tools can approach AI's scientific competence, because human collaboration is bottlenecked by individual pattern intuition and the tiny pipeline of person-to-person explanation — AI can work with vast diffuse patterns without compressing them.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The rebuttal that matters: even a saturating-intelligence AI beats human teams because it escapes communication bandwidth limits, preserving the case for AI-native research organizations.
insights.locator: If this turns out to be true, it means Francois Chollet is wrong.

insights.claim: Even if AI never gets much better than humans at the science humans already do, it might open whole realms of discovery inaccessible to even the largest groups of the smartest humans.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Decouples AI's scientific value from benchmark superiority, meaning capability plateaus are not evidence against an AI-driven research boom.
insights.locator: So even if AI never gets much better than humans

insights.claim: The common thread is that AI may revolutionize productivity not by being much smarter than any individual human but by marrying human-style intelligence to the vast, inhuman capabilities of computers — speed, memory, sensor interfacing and detail perception.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Shifts the diligence question from 'how smart is the model' to 'how much data throughput and system integration does the product exploit' — a different set of winners.
insights.quote: AI may revolutionize productivity not by being much smarter than a single individual human — not by simply solving harder and harder math problems — but by marrying human-style intelligence to the vast, inhuman capabilities of computers.
insights.locator: The common thread in all three of these examples

insights.claim: We may be thinking about the benefits of intelligence wrong — arrogantly privileging the mental tasks humans happen to do especially well while ignoring the value of the tasks we do poorly.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Suggests the largest AI value pools sit in tasks humans are bad at and therefore under-measure — an under-covered category for capital allocation.
insights.locator: We could simply be thinking about the benefits of intelligence wrong

insights.claim: There is a widespread tacit assumption among intelligent people that the quality which made them stand out among their peers is the fundamental stuff of the universe and the font of all value, which helps explain why treating intelligence as just one production factor among many seems unthinkable and heretical in the tech industry.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A behavioural explanation for systematic bias in AI forecasting by insiders — useful when discounting practitioner projections of takeoff.
insights.locator: Footnote 3

insights.claim: Mathematicians are not expected to lose their jobs en masse even as AI surpasses them, because tenure exists, humans are needed to understand what AI produces, human teachers remain valuable, and most importantly humans must tell AI what math to solve and why.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Task-direction and verification remain human roles even in fully automated domains, which is where residual employment and pricing power concentrate.
insights.locator: Footnote 1
